newsitem.title: COLOMBIA: Colombian lawmakers probe ex-president Gaviria.
newsitem.headline: Colombian lawmakers probe ex-president Gaviria.

text.p: Former President Cesar Gaviria said he met a group of Colombian lawmakers in Washington on Tuesday to answer questions about alleged misconduct when he served as head of state from 1990-94.

Gaviria, now secretary-general of the Organisation of American States, said the preliminary investigation was broadly focused on "some of the actions of my government that provoked certain controversy" at the time they were committed.

He told Colombian journalists at OAS headquarters in Washington that congressional investigators were seeking to determine whether his administration was responsible for any "deliberate violation of the constitution or the law."

Among other actions, he said congressional investigators were looking into the reasons behind his decision to convoke a constituent assembly in 1991 and to provide amnesty to a former guerrilla leader so he could participate in the rewriting of Colombia's constitution.

Congressional sources said lawmakers were also investigating charges that Gaviria violated Colombia's sovereignty in 1993 when he authorised U.S. troops to carry out a so-called civic action programme involving the construction of a school and roadway in a jungle-covered area of southwest Valle province.

Gaviria faces similar violation of sovereignty charges, the sources said, for authorising U.S. spy planes to overfly the infamous La Catedral prison in northwest Antioquia province where late Medellin cartel drug boss Pablo Escobar was held in luxurious conditions from June 1991 until his escape in July 1992.

The palatial living conditions inside La Catedral, which Escobar had custom-built for himself and from which he continued to run his criminal empire, sparked a public outcry when they finally became known after his escape.

The five lawmakers who travelled to Washington are members of the Committee of Accusations of the House of Representatives, the same panel that investigated charges that President Ernesto Samper used drug money to finance his 1994 election campaign. Committee members voted twice, by an overwhelming majority, to shelve that investigation.
